Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 1:

(p-203) Surat al-Hadid

Meccan, though it is said to be Medinan; its verses are twenty-nine.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah.﴾ At-tasbih (glorification, the declaring of Allah's transcendence) is exalting Allah, the Exalted, in belief, speech and action, above whatever is unfitting for His majesty. It derives from sabaha in the earth and on the water, meaning he went off and went far in them. Here it is attributed to non-rational beings as well, since "whatever is in the heavens and the earth" encompasses everything in them, whether it dwells in them or is a part of them, as was mentioned in the verse of the Throne. It is intended in a general, metaphorical sense that includes what glorifies by the tongue of speech, such as the glorification of the angels and the believers among the two species (jinn and humankind), and what glorifies by the tongue of state, such as the glorification of others. Every individual existent points, by its contingency and its having come into being, to the eternal Creator, the Necessarily Existent, characterized by perfection and free from deficiency. This is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there is not a thing but that it glorifies [Him] with His praise﴾. The verb is transitive by itself, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and glorify Him﴾. The lam (ل) is either superfluous for emphasis, as in "I advised him" (nasahtu lahu) and "I thanked him" (shakartu lahu), or it marks cause, meaning: he performed the glorification for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, and sincerely for His countenance. Its occurrence in some of the opening surahs in the past tense and in others in the present tense indicates its certainty at all times. This also alerts that whoever is capable of voluntary glorification ought to glorify Him, exalted is He, at all times, as the exalted assembly does, glorifying night and day without slackening.

﴿And He is the Almighty﴾: the Capable, the Overpowering, whom nothing prevents or contends with.

﴿the All-Wise﴾: who does only what wisdom and benefit require. The sentence is a concluding interjection (i'tiraḍ tadhyīlī) that confirms the meaning of what precedes it and indicates the cause of the ruling. Likewise His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 2:

﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. That is: the absolute disposal over them and over what is in them of existing things, in terms of bringing into being and annihilating, and all other kinds of disposal, whether of what we know and what we do not know. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence not grammatically linked to what precedes) explaining some of the rulings of dominion and disposal. Making it a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "lahu" (to Him) is not as it should be.

﴿And He is over all things﴾ among the things of which what has been mentioned, namely giving life and causing death, is a part.

﴿Powerful (qadir)﴾, one who is intensive (mubaligh) in power.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 3:

﴿He is the First﴾ — the One who precedes all existent things, because He is their originator (mubdi') and their innovator (mubdi').

Note: the Arabic here reads "mubdi'uha wa-mubdi'uha," and the translation above is given as follows: He is their originator (mubdi') and their innovator (mubdi').

Correction to the above, rendered faithfully:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 3:

﴿He is the First﴾ — the One who precedes all existent things (al-sabiq 'ala sa'ir al-mawjudat), because He is their originator (mubdi'uha) and their innovator (mubdi'uha).

﴿And the Last﴾ — the One who remains after their annihilation (fana'iha), in reality, or in consideration of His essence, setting aside His sustaining them (mubqihi). For all possible existent things, when consideration of their cause is set aside, are perishing (fania).

﴿And the Manifest﴾ — in existence, due to the abundance of His clear proofs (dala'ilihi al-wadiha). (p-204)

﴿And the Hidden﴾ — in reality, so that minds do not circle around Him. The first waw and the last waw are for the conjunction of the two attributes flanking them, and the middle waw is for the conjunction of the two groups. Thus He is characterized by the continuity of existence at all times, and by manifestness and hiddenness.

﴿And He is, of everything, Knowing﴾ — nothing escapes His knowledge, of the manifest or the hidden.

﴿He it is who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne﴾: an explanation of some of the rulings concerning His dominion over them both. Its interpretation has passed several times.

﴿He knows what enters into the earth and what comes out of it, and what descends from the sky and what ascends into it﴾: its explanation has passed in Surat Saba'.

﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾: an illustration of the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of them, and a depiction of their not being outside it wherever they turn. His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ is an expression for His encompassing their deeds. Its being placed after the creation is because what is meant by it is the knowledge upon which recompense revolves, which follows the known [object], not because of what has been said, that it is an indication of it [the creation].

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 5:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a repetition for emphasis and a preparation for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and to Allah all matters are returned﴾. That is: to Him alone, not to anyone else, either independently or jointly, all matters are returned. It is read with the passive voice, from rajaʻa (tura'ja'u... ), "turja'u" (تُرْجَعُ), and it has been read in the active voice, from rajaʻa rujūʻan (رَجَعَ رُجُوعًا).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 6:

﴿He causes the night to enter into the day, and He causes the day to enter into the night﴾. Its interpretation has passed several times. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He is All-Knowing﴾, meaning: exceedingly knowing (mubaligh fi al-'ilm).

﴿of what is within the breasts﴾, meaning: of its inherent hidden contents. It is an explanation of the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of what they conceal of their intentions, after the explanation of His comprehensiveness of their deeds which they display.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 7:

﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger, and spend from that of which He has made you successors (mustakhlafin).﴾ That is: He has made you vicegerents (khulafa') in disposing of it, without your owning it in reality. He expressed what is in their hands of wealth and provisions in this way, to affirm the truth and to encourage them to spend. For whoever knows that it belongs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that he is only like a trustee (wakil) who disposes of it in the channels which Allah Most High has appointed, spending becomes easy for him. Or it means: He has made you successors to those before you in what was in their hands, by its being inherited by you. So take warning from their condition, for it passed from them to you, and it will pass from you to those after you. So do not be stingy with it.

﴿So those of you who believe and spend﴾ as they were commanded.

﴿For them﴾ by virtue of that.

﴿is a great reward﴾ In it there is of emphasis what is not hidden: he made it a nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya), the mention of belief and spending is repeated, the predication is reinforced, the reward is magnified by indefiniteness (al-tankir) and described as great.

The Almighty and Majestic's words: ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not believe in God?﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence that follows on from what precedes it), brought to rebuke them for abandoning faith, as they were commanded to, and to deny that they have any excuse whatsoever. The phrase ﴿lā tu'minūn﴾ (you do not believe) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in ﴿lakum﴾ (for you), and the element governing it is the sense of stability (istiqrār) contained in the preposition. The meaning is: "What has happened to you, while you are unbelievers?" The denial and negation are directed at the cause alone, while the effect is established, not at the cause and the effect together. This is like His words: ﴿And what is [the matter] with me that I do not worship He who originated me?﴾ For the interrogative hamza (hamzat al-istifhām) sometimes denies an occurring act, as in "Do you strike your father?", and sometimes denies that an act has occurred, as in "Shall I strike my father?" Likewise, the interrogative ﴿mā﴾ (what) may deny and negate only the cause of an occurring act, as in our present case and in His words: ﴿What is [the matter] with you that you do not hope for dignity from God?﴾ In that case the content of the circumstantial clause is established, since both the absence of faith and the absence of hope are realities which have been denied and whose cause has been negated. It may also deny and negate the cause of an event, and the denial then extends to the effect as well, as in His words: ﴿And what is [the matter] with me that I do not worship…﴾ to the end of the verse. In that case the content of the circumstantial clause is assumed to be certainly non-existent, since the absence of worship is a matter presumed to be necessary, whose cause has been denied and negated, so that the thing itself is also negated. His words: ﴿while the Messenger calls you to believe in your Lord﴾ form a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun in ﴿lā tu'minūn﴾, serving to rebuke them for disbelief, given that what necessitates its absence is established, after they have been rebuked for it, while what would necessitate it is absent. That is: "And what excuse do you have for abandoning faith, when the Messenger calls you to it and admonishes you concerning it?" His words: ﴿and He has already taken your covenant﴾ form a circumstantial clause relating to the object of ﴿yad'ūkum﴾ (calls you), meaning: God the Exalted has already taken your covenant to believe, previously, and this was done by setting up the proofs and enabling you to reflect. It has also been read as ﴿wa-qad ukhidha﴾ in the passive voice, with ﴿mīthāqakum﴾ (your covenant) in the nominative case.

﴿if you are believers﴾: the requirement (mūjib) is this, for this is a requirement beyond which there is no further requirement.

He is the One who sends down upon His servant (Muhammad ﷺ) clear signs, as He sees fit for you of benefits.

﴿آيَاتٍ بَيِّنَاتٍ﴾ — manifest, clear.

﴿لِيُخْرِجَكُمْ﴾ — that He may bring you out; i.e., Allah the Exalted, or the servant by means of them.

﴿مِنَ الظُّلُمَاتِ إِلَى النُّورِ﴾ — from the darkness of disbelief into the light of faith.

﴿وَإِنَّ اللَّهَ بِكُمْ لَرَءُوفٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ — in that He guides you to the happiness of both abodes, by sending the Messenger and sending down the signs after the establishment of rational proofs.

(p-206)

And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And what is [wrong] with you that you do not spend in the way of Allah?﴾ It is a rebuke to them for abandoning the spending that they were commanded to do, following their rebuke for abandoning faith, by denying that they have any excuse whatsoever in that either. The object is omitted because it is evident that it is the thing whose state was explained earlier, and specifying what is to be spent upon is for the intensification of the rebuke. That is: "And what reason do you have for not spending on that which is an act of drawing near to Allah, the Exalted, which in reality is His [property], while you are only His stewards in disposing of it to the channels He has designated?"

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the subject of "do not spend" and its object, and it serves to reinforce the rebuke. For abandoning spending without a cause is reprehensible and objectionable, and when that which obligates spending is established, it is even more reprehensible and more emphatically denounced. The statement that all the wealth in the heavens and the earth will remain, in the Hereafter, to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, after none of its owners remains, is more forceful in obligating spending upon them than the statement that it belongs to Allah, Exalted, in reality, while they are His stewards in disposing of it. It is as if it were said: "And what reason do you have in abandoning spending it in the way of Allah, when in fact none of it will remain for you, but all of it will remain for Allah, Exalted?" The placing of the noble Name in the position of a pronoun serves to increase the affirmation and to instill awe.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest﴾ is an explanation that the ranks of the spenders differ according to the differences in their states in spending, after the explanation that they have a great reward absolutely, urging them to seek out what is most excellent. The conjoining of fighting with spending is to indicate that it is among the most important materials of spending, along with it being in itself among the best acts of worship, and that it is never free of spending at all. The counterpart of "those who spent" is omitted because of its evidence and because what follows indicates it. It was also read as "qabla al-fath" without "min." The conquest is the conquest of Makkah.

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to "those who spent." The plural is in view of the meaning of "man" (those), just as the singularity of the two preceding pronouns is in view of its wording, along with what it contains of the sense of distance, despite the nearness of the time of the one referred to, to indicate the remoteness of their station and the loftiness of their rank in excellence. Its position is nominative, as the subject of a nominal sentence: that is, "those who are described with these two beautiful attributes."

﴿Greater in rank﴾ and higher in station.

﴿than those who spent afterward and fought﴾ because they did what they did of spending and fighting before the might of Islam and the strength of its people, at a time of the utmost need for support with self and wealth. They are the foremost, earliest of the Emigrants and the Helpers, about whom the Prophet ﷺ said: "If one of you were to spend the equivalent of Mount Uhud in gold, it would not reach a mudd of one of them, nor half of it." Those others did what they did after the religion had become manifest and people had entered it in multitudes, and when the need for spending and fighting had diminished.

﴿And to each﴾ that is, each of the two groups.

﴿Allah has promised the best﴾ that is, the best reward, which is Paradise, not only to the first group.It was also read "wa kullun" with a nominative ending, as a subject: that is, "and each one, Allah has promised him [the best]."

﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ with its outward and inward aspects, and He will recompense you according to it. It has been said that the verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, for he was the first to believe, the first to spend in the way of Allah, and he contended with the disbelievers until he was struck a blow that brought him close to death.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 11:

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan﴾, it is an emphatic exhortation from Allah, Exalted is He, to spend in His cause after the command to do so, the rebuke for abandoning it, and the explanation of the ranks of those who spend. That is: who is it that spends his wealth in His cause, Exalted is He, hoping that He will compensate him, for that is like one who lends to Him. The goodness of spending lies in sincerity in it and in seeking out the noblest wealth and the best of avenues.

﴿So that He may multiply it for him﴾ is read with the accusative (fa-yudā'ifahu), as a response to the interrogative in terms of meaning, as if it were said: Will anyone lend to Allah so that He multiplies it for him? That is: so that He gives him his reward manifold.

﴿And for him is a noble reward﴾. That is: that reward, to which the multiplication is added, is noble in itself, worthy of being sought eagerly by those who seek eagerly, and even if it were not multiplied, how much more so when it has been multiplied many times over. It is also read in the nominative, either as a conjunction with "yuqriḍu" or as a sentence with an implied subject, meaning: so He multiplies it for him. It is also read as "yuḍʿifahu," in both the nominative and the accusative.

﴿On the day you see the believing men and believing women﴾ is an adverbial complement (ẓarf, an adverb of time) modifying either the phrase ﴿and for him is a noble reward﴾ or the phrase ﴿so that He may multiply it﴾. Alternatively, it is in the accusative by an implied "remember" (idmar "udhkur"), to magnify that day. The phrase ﴿their light runs before them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal, a circumstantial accusative) of the object of "you see." It is said that their light is the radiance that is seen ﴿before them and on their right hands﴾. It is also said that it is their guidance, and "on their right hands" refers to their books, meaning: their faith and righteous deeds run before them, and the books of their deeds are in their right hands. It is also said that the light is the Qur'an. From Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him): they will be given their light according to the measure of their deeds. Some of them will be given a light like a palm tree, and some will be given a light like a man standing. The one with the least light will have a light on the big toe of his foot, which goes out at times and flashes at others. Al-Hasan said: "They will be guided by it over the Sirat." Muqatil said: "It will be for them a guide to Paradise."

﴿Your glad tidings today are gardens﴾ is implied by a verb of saying, and it is either a circumstantial clause (hal) or a resumptive new sentence (isti'naf). That is, it is said to them: "Your glad tidings," meaning: what you are given good news of is gardens. Or: your glad tidings is the entry into Paradise.

﴿beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein﴾ — that is, what has been mentioned of the light and the glad tidings of the everlasting gardens.

﴿That is the great triumph﴾ — the triumph beyond which there is no further end. It has also been read as "That is the great triumph."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 13:

﴿The Day the hypocrite men and hypocrite women say﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the Day you see".

﴿to those who believe: "Wait for us (unzurūnā)"﴾ That is: wait for us (intaẓirūnā). They say this because the believers are hastened to Paradise like a flashing lightning on mounts that escort them, while these are on foot. Or it means: look at us (unẓurū ilaynā), for when the believers look at them, they face them with their faces and thereby are illumined by the light that is before them. It was also read "anẓirūnā" (give us respite), from al-nazra, which is respite (al-imhāl); their slowness in proceeding until they reach them is taken as a respite granted to them.

﴿"We will borrow from your light"﴾ That is: we will be illumined by it, and its root meaning is taking a qabas (a firebrand, a burning coal).

﴿It will be said﴾ as a dismissal of them and a mockery of them, from the side of the believers, or from the side of the angels.

﴿"Turn back behind you"﴾ That is: to the place of standing (al-mawqif).

﴿"Then seek a light"﴾ For it is from there that light is borrowed. Or: back to the world, then seek the light by acquiring its beginnings from faith and righteous deeds. Or: "Turn back, disappointed and rejected, then seek another light." They knew that there was no light behind them, and they only said it to disappoint them. Or they meant by "light" the thick darkness behind them, mocking them.

﴿Then a wall was set up between them﴾ between the two groups.

﴿with a gate⁠﻿ (sūr)﴾ That is: a barrier (ḥā'iṭ), and the bāʾ is superfluous.

﴿Its inner side has a gate, within which is mercy﴾ That is: the inner side of the wall or of the gate, which is the side facing Paradise.

﴿and its outer side, from before it, is punishment﴾ which is the part facing the Fire, "from its direction" (min jihatihi).

﴿punishment﴾ It was also read "fa-ḍaraba" in the active voice.

(p-208)﴿They will call out to them﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*, a new sentence that answers an implied question) built upon a question, as if it were said: "What will they do after the wall is set up and they witness the punishment?" It was answered: "They will call out to them."

﴿Were we not with you?﴾ In the world.

﴿With you﴾ They mean by this their agreeing with them outwardly.

﴿They will say: "Yes"﴾ You were with us according to outward appearance, ﴿but you tempted yourselves﴾ you put them to the test with hypocrisy and destroyed them.

﴿And you waited﴾ for the believers to suffer misfortunes (*al-dawa'ir*).

﴿And you doubted﴾ concerning the matter of the religion.

﴿And false desires deluded you﴾ which are empty, and among which is the hope that the affair of Islam would be overturned.

﴿Until the command of God came﴾ that is, death.

﴿And the Deceiver deluded you concerning God﴾ the Generous.

﴿The Deceiver﴾ that is, Satan deluded you into thinking that God is Forgiving and Generous and will not punish you. It is also recited as "al-Ghurur" (*al-Ghurur*) with a dammah on the first letter, which is a variant reading.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 15:

﴿Today no ransom will be taken from you﴾, i.e., no compensation (fida'), and it has been recited as "tu'khadhu" with a ta' (feminine prefix).

﴿Nor from those who disbelieved﴾, i.e., outwardly and inwardly.

﴿Your abode is the Fire﴾: you will never depart from it.

﴿It is your protector (mawlakum)﴾, i.e., it has more right over you (awla bikum). Its literal sense is "your place," about which it is said: "He is more deserving of you," just as it is said: "He is mi'natu al-karam," meaning a place for the saying of the speaker that he is indeed generous. Or it means: your place near to the wali (closeness), that is, nearness. Or it means: your helper, following the manner of the saying: [Their greeting among them is a painful blow]. Or it means: your guardian, who takes charge of you just as you took charge of its requirements.

﴿And wretched is the destination﴾, i.e., the Fire.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 16:

﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of Allah?﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnaf) that rebukes them for their sluggishness in matters of religion and their weakness in holding to them, and it expresses surprise at their slowness in responding to what they were urged towards through encouragement and warning. It is narrated that the believers were in hardship in Makkah, and when they emigrated they obtained provision and blessing and grew lax in what they had been doing, so this verse was revealed. It is also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) that the time between our acceptance of Islam and being reproached with this verse was only four years. And it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that Allah was slow to see the hearts of the believers, so He reproached them at the end of thirteen years from the revelation of the Qur'an. The meaning is: Has the time not come for their hearts to humble themselves to the remembrance of Him, exalted is He, to find rest in it, and to hasten to obey Him by carrying out His commands and abstaining from what He has forbidden, without delay or slackness? It comes from "anā al-amr" (the matter arrived), meaning when it came, its time (ināhu), that is, its appointed time. It is also read "alam yaʾin" from "āna yaʾīnu," with the meaning of "anā" (Arabic: أنى). It is read "alammā yaʾni" (Arabic: ألَمّا يَأنِ), and this indicates that the negated matter is expected.

﴿and what has been revealed of the truth﴾: that is, the Qur'an. It is conjoined to "the remembrance of Allah." If the remembrance of Allah is also meant here, then the conjunction is due to the difference between the two designations, since it is both a remembrance and an admonition, just as it is a truth sent down from heaven. Otherwise the conjunction is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The believers are only those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith﴾. The meaning of humility (khushuʿ) before Him is complete submission to His commands and prohibitions, and devotion to acting upon what is in it of rulings, among which are what precedes and what follows concerning spending in the way of Allah, exalted is He. It is read "nazzala" from tanzil (Arabic: التنزيل) in the passive voice and in the active voice, and "unzila."

﴿And that they should not be like those who were given the Book before, ...﴾ This is conjoined to "takhsha'" (should humble themselves). It is read with the "ta" (Arabic: بِالتَّاءِ) as an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person, Arabic: الِالتِفاتِ) to give emphasis to the warning. It has been said that it is a prohibition against resembling the People of the Book in the hardening of hearts after they had been rebuked. This is because the Children of Israel, when the truth stood between them and their desires, and when they heard the Torah and the Gospel, would humble themselves before Allah and their hearts would soften.

﴿So the term grew long for them﴾: that is, the time period. It is read "al-amadd" (Arabic: الأمَدُّ) with a doubled "dal," meaning the longest period. Harshness overcame them, and the awe that used to come to them from the two Books departed from them.

﴿So their hearts became hardened﴾: they are like stones, or even harder in hardness.

﴿And many of them are defiant transgressors﴾: that is, they went outside the limits of their religion, rejecting entirely what is in their Book.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 17:

﴿Know that Allah revives the earth after its death.﴾ This is an illustration (tamthil) of the reviving of hardened hearts through remembrance (dhikr) and recitation, by means of the reviving of dead land through rain, to encourage humility (khushu') and to warn against hardness of heart (qasawa).

﴿We have indeed made the signs clear to you﴾, of which these verses are among the whole.

﴿So that you may understand (la'allakum ta'qilun)﴾: so that you might comprehend what is in them and act in accordance with their requirements, and thereby attain the happiness of both abodes.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 18:

﴿Indeed, the male almsgivers and the female almsgivers﴾ That is: the men who give charity (al-mutasaddiqin) and the women who give charity (al-mutasaddiqat). It has also been read thus, and it has been read with the sad lightened from tasdiq (belief in the truth), that is: those who affirmed Allah and His Messenger.

﴿and who have lent to Allah a goodly loan﴾ It has been said: this is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon what is in al-mussaddiqin of the meaning of the verb, for it is in the ruling of "those who gave charity" or "those who affirmed," according to the two readings. It was objected that this involves separating the parts of the relative clause (silah) by a foreign element, namely al-mussaddiqat. It was answered that the meaning is: the people who gave charity, and the women who gave charity, and who lent; so it is a conjunction upon the relative clause in meaning, without any separation. It has also been said that al-mussaddiqat is not a conjunction upon al-mussaddiqin, but is in the accusative by specification (al-ikhtisas), as if it were said: "Indeed the almsgivers in general, by way of predominance (taghlib), and I single out the women among them," just as you say: "Indeed those who believe, especially the scholars among them, and who do righteous deeds, for them is such-and-such." However, not on the basis that the ground of the specification is the greater deserving of the women for doubled reward, as in the example mentioned, but rather the greater need of the women for giving charity, which calls for special attention to urging them to give charity, based on what has been narrated: that he, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "O assembly of women, give charity, for I have been shown that most of the people of the Fire are you." It has also been said: it is a relative clause for a deleted relative noun conjoined upon the almsgivers, as if it were said: "and those who lent the goodly loan," which is an expression for charity from good things, given from a contented soul and sincere intention, to one deserving of charity.

﴿It will be multiplied for them﴾ It is read in the passive voice, with what follows it of the prepositional phrase as its subject. It has also been said: it is attributed to a verbal noun of what is in the relative clause's domain, with a deleted modifier, that is: the reward of charity. It has also been read in the active voice, that is: Allah the Exalted multiplies it. It has also been read yudaʿʿafu, with the ʿayn doubled and vowelled with a fatha.

﴿And for them is a noble reward﴾ What is in it of discussion has passed.

**(p-210)** Those who believe in God and His messengers, **all of them**. The manner of believing in them has already been explained at the end of Surat al-Baqarah.

**﴿Ulā'ika﴾** ("those") is a demonstrative referring to the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*, "those who"), which is the subject (*mubtada'*, "the topic" of the nominal sentence). The sense of distance contained in it, despite the recent mention of its referent, has been explained many times before. It is the second subject (*mubtada' thani*). The words of God Most High, **﴿hum﴾** ("they"), are a third subject (*mubtada' thalith*) whose predicate (*khabar*, "the comment") is **﴿al-siddiqun wa-al-shuhada'﴾** ("the truthful and the martyrs"). This, together with its predicate, is the predicate of the second subject, and that, together with its predicate, is the predicate of the first subject. Alternatively, **"hum"** is a separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*, "the pronoun of separation"), and what follows it is the predicate of **"ulā'ika,"** and the whole clause is the predicate of the relative pronoun. That is, **﴿ulā'ika ʿinda rabbihim﴾** ("those are with their Lord"), in the rank of the truthful and the martyrs, who are renowned for their exalted station and elevated position. They are those who were foremost in affirming the truth and who were killed in the way of God Most High. Or, they are those who are most sincere in truthfulness, in that they believed in and affirmed all of God Most High's reports and His messengers, and who bear witness to God Most High's oneness and to their own faith. Or, they are those who will bear witness against the nations on the Day of Resurrection.

The words of God Most High, **﴿lahum ajruhum wa-nurahum﴾** ("for them is their reward and their light"), explain the fruits of the qualities of perfection by which they were described. This is a clause composed of a subject and predicate, situated in the nominative case, as a second predicate of the relative pronoun. Or the predicate is the prepositional phrase (*al-jarr wa-ma ba'dahu*, "the preposition and what follows it"), and what follows it is raised by it as the agent (*fa'iliyya*). The first pronoun, according to the first interpretation, refers to the relative pronoun, and the last two refer to the truthful and the martyrs. That is, **"mithl ajrihim wa-nurihim"** ("like their reward and their light"), which are known for the utmost perfection and the difficulty of attainment. He omitted the particle of comparison as an alert to the strength of the resemblance and its reaching the limit of identity, just as He did when it was said: **"hum al-siddiqun wa-al-shuhada'"** ("they are the truthful and the martyrs"). The resemblance is not between what the first group has of reward and light and the complete amount of what the first has of principal and multiples, nor between what the last two have of principal without multiples. As for the second interpretation, the reference of all of it is one, and the meaning is: for them are the reward and the light promised to them, **"lahum ajruhum ..."** ("for them is their reward...") and so on.

**﴿Wa-alladhina kafaru wa-kadhdhabu bi-ayatina ulā'ika﴾** ("And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, those are"), the ones described with that ugly attribute.

**﴿Ashab al-jahim﴾** ("the companions of the Hellfire"), such that they will never depart from it, ever.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 20:

﴿Know that the life of this world is but play and amusement, adornment and boasting among yourselves, and competition in wealth and children.﴾ After having explained the state of the two groups in the Hereafter, it explains the state of the worldly life, in which the second group found comfort. It is indicated that it is among the trivial matters on which the intelligent do not rely, let alone find peace in them; and that, despite this, it is swift to pass away and quick to perish, as it is said: ﴿like the example of rain whose vegetation pleases the disbelievers﴾, i.e., the farmers.

﴿its vegetation﴾, i.e., the plant produced by it.

﴿then it dries up﴾, i.e., it withers after its greenness and freshness.

﴿and you see it turned yellow﴾ after you had seen it fresh and beautiful. It is also read "muṣfārran". The phrase "then it turns yellow" is not used, to signal that its yellowing accompanies its drying, and what follows from it is that it is seen in that state.

﴿then it becomes debris﴾, i.e., broken, crumbled stubble. As for the place of the kaf (in "kamathali"), it is said to be in the accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl) clause referring to the pronoun in "la'ibun", because it carries the sense of a description. It is also said to be in the nominative, as a second predicate for "lil-ḥayāh al-dunyā", with an omitted modifier, i.e., "the example of the life of this world is like the example of ...", etc. Having shown the insignificance of the worldly affair, to make one averse to it and to deter one from clinging to it, the magnificence of the matter of the Hereafter and the greatness of the pleasures and pains in it are indicated, to encourage the attainment of its everlasting bliss and to warn against (p-211) its painful punishment. The punishment has been mentioned, saying: ﴿and in the Hereafter there is severe punishment﴾, because it is one of the results of being absorbed in what has been detailed about the worldly life.

﴿and forgiveness﴾, great,

﴿from Allah, and approval﴾, great, whose worth cannot be measured.

﴿And the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion﴾, i.e., for one who finds comfort in it and does not make it a means to the Hereafter. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "The world is the enjoyment of delusion; if it distracts you from seeking the Hereafter, then it is (merely delusion). But if it calls you to seeking the approval of Allah the Exalted, then it is a fine enjoyment and a fine means."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 21:

﴿Race﴾ i.e., hasten with the eagerness of those who compete with their peers on the racecourse (al-midmar).

﴿To forgiveness﴾ great, coming to be ﴿from your Lord﴾, i.e., toward the things that necessitate it (mujibat) from righteous deeds.

﴿And a Garden whose breadth is like the breadth of the heaven and the earth﴾ i.e., like their breadth altogether. And if its breadth is thus, then what do you suppose of its length? It was also said: the intended meaning of "breadth" ('ard) is expanse (al-bastah). The mention of forgiveness before the Garden is because clearing (al-takhliyah) precedes adorning (al-tahliyah).

﴿Prepared for those who believe in Allah and His messengers﴾ In this is evidence that the Garden is already created, and that faith alone is sufficient for entitlement to it.

﴿That﴾ which was promised of forgiveness and the Garden.

﴿Is the bounty of Allah﴾ His giving.

﴿He bestows it﴾ out of graciousness and kindness.

﴿upon whom He wills﴾ granting it to him without any obligation.

﴿And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾ and for this reason He bestows the like of that bounty, which has no limit beyond it, upon whom He wills.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 22:

﴿No affliction befalls in the earth﴾ such as drought and blight in the crops and fruits.

﴿Nor in yourselves﴾ such as sickness and calamity.

﴿Except in a Book﴾ i.e., except that it is written down and recorded in the knowledge of Allah the Exalted or in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh).

﴿Before We bring it into being﴾ i.e., before We create the souls, the afflictions, or the earth.

﴿Indeed that﴾ i.e., its recording in a Book.

﴿Is easy for Allah﴾ because He, in this matter, is free of need for preparation (al-'uddah) and time (al-muddah).

﴿So that you do not despair﴾ means: We informed you of this so that you would not grieve.

﴿over what has escaped you﴾ of the blessings of this world.

﴿and do not exult in what He has given you﴾ means: what Allah the Exalted has bestowed upon you of it. For whoever knows that everything is predestined, that what was decreed to be lost will be lost, and that what was decreed to come will certainly come, his anxiety over what has passed will not be great, nor will his joy in what is coming. It is also read as "bima ataakum" (بِما أتاكُمْ), from the verb "ityan" (الإتيان, coming). In the first reading (bima ataakum, بِما آتاكُمْ, from "ataa," to give) there is an indication that the loss of blessings befalls them when they are left to their own nature, whereas their presence and continuance require a cause that brings them into being and sustains them. It is also read as "bima ut-itum" (بِما أُوتِيتُمْ, from the passive of "ataa"). The intended meaning is the negation of the grief that prevents submission to the decree of Allah the Exalted, and of the joy that produces insolence and self-conceit. For this reason it is followed by His saying: ﴿Allah does not love any arrogant boaster﴾, for whoever rejoices in worldly portions and they grow great in his soul will inevitably become conceited and boastful over them. The specification of this concluding remark with the prohibition against the mentioned joy indicates that it is more blameworthy than grief.(p-212)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 24:

﴿Those who are miserly and enjoin miserliness upon people﴾ is in apposition (badal) to ﴿every arrogant boaster﴾, for the one who is proud of his wealth generally withholds it and commands others to do the same. Or it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is omitted, indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever turns away, then indeed Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾. Its meaning is: whoever turns away from spending, then indeed Allah is free of need of him and of his spending, praiseworthy in His essence, not harmed by the turning away from His thanks by drawing near to Him with some of His blessings. In this there is a threat and an indication that the command to spend is for the benefit of the one who spends. It has also been read as "fa-inna Allaha al-Ghaniyyu" (with the definite article on al-Ghaniyy).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 25:**

﴿We certainly sent Our messengers﴾: that is, the angels to the prophets, or the prophets to the nations, and this is the more apparent (al-azhar).

﴿with clear proofs﴾: that is, with arguments (hujaj) and miracles (mu'jizat).

﴿And We sent down with them the Book﴾: that is, the category of Book, which encompasses all of them.

﴿and the Balance, so that people may uphold justice﴾: that is, with equity (al-'adl). It is related that Jibril (peace be upon him) descended with the Balance and gave it to Nuh (peace be upon him), saying: "Command your people to weigh with it." It has also been said: what is meant by it is justice, so that governance (al-siyasa) may be established by it and aggression repelled by it.

﴿And We sent down iron﴾: It has been said that Adam (peace be upon him) descended from the Garden with five iron implements: the anvil (al-sindan), the two tongs (al-kalbatan), the hammer-stand (al-miqa'a), the hammer (al-mitraqa), and the needle (al-ibra). It is also related that he had with him the adze (al-marr) and the shovel (al-misha). And from al-Hasan: "And We sent down iron" means "We created it," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He sent down for you of the cattle﴾, because His commands, decrees and judgments descend from the heavens. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in it is great might﴾, because instruments of war are only made from it.

﴿and benefits for people﴾: since there is no craft except that iron, or what is worked from iron, is its tool. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the iron. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that Allah may know who supports Him and His messengers﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon an implied element indicated by what precedes it, for it is a circumstantial clause implying causation, as if it were said: "so that they may use it, and so that Allah may know with a knowledge on which reward depends, who supports Him and His messenger by using swords, spears and all other weapons in striving against His enemies." Or it is connected to a delayed implied element, and the waw is parenthetical (i'tiradiyya), meaning: "And so that Allah may know who supports Him and His messengers, [He sent it down]." It has also been said that it is conjoined to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that people may uphold justice﴾. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿unseen﴾ is a circumstantial clause relating either to the subject of "supports" or to its object, meaning: "absent from them" or "absent from Him." His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed Allah is Strong, Mighty﴾ is a concluding parenthetical clause (i'tiraDh tadhyili), brought to affirm the truth and to alert that imposing jihad upon them and exposing them to fighting is not because He needs them to elevate His word and manifest His religion, but rather it is so that they may benefit from it and, by complying with the command concerning it, attain reward; otherwise He is free of need of them through His power and might in everything He wills.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 26:

﴿And We certainly sent Noah and Abraham﴾ is a kind of detailing of what was summarized in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers﴾ ...etc. The repetition of the oath serves to show greater care for the matter; that is, by Allah, We certainly sent the two of them.

﴿And We placed in their offspring prophethood and the Book﴾ by Our having made them prophets and having revealed the Books to them. It has also been said that what is meant by "the Book" is writing with the pen (al-khatt bil-qalam).

﴿Among them﴾ that is, among the offspring, or among those to whom the messengers were sent, which is indicated by the mention of sending and messengers.

﴿is one who is guided﴾ to the truth.

﴿And many of them are defiant transgressors﴾ who have deviated from the straight path. The departure from the pattern of the contrast (i.e., not saying "and many of them are disbelievers" in a parallel form) is for the sake of intensifying the condemnation and signaling the dominance and multitude of the misguided.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 57, verse 27:

﴿Then We caused Our messengers to follow in their footsteps.﴾ That is: then We sent Our messengers after them.

﴿And We caused Jesus, son of Mary, to follow.﴾ That is: We sent one messenger after another until it reached Jesus, son of Mary, peace be upon him. The pronoun refers to Noah, Abraham, and those to whom they were sent, or to the messengers who were contemporaries of them, not to the offspring (dhurriyyah), for the messengers who were followed were among the offspring.

﴿And We gave him the Injil (Gospel).﴾ It is also read with a fatha on the hamza (إنْجَيلَ), since it is a non-Arabic word (a'jami), and so it is not required to conform to the patterns (abniyah) of Arabic.

﴿And We placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion (ra'fah).﴾ It is also read as "ra'afah" (رَآفَةً) on the pattern fa'alah.

﴿And mercy (rahmah).﴾ That is: We enabled them to show mercy and affection toward one another. Similar is His saying about the companions of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "compassionate among themselves" (﴿رُحَماءُ بَيْنَهُمْ﴾).

﴿And monasticism (rahbaniyyah), which they invented.﴾ This is in the accusative case, either governed by a verb understood, which the following word explains, meaning: "and they invented monasticism, ﴿which they invented﴾"; or by coordination with what precedes it, and "which they invented" is an adjective for it, meaning: "And We placed in their hearts compassion, mercy, and invented monasticism originating from themselves," that is: "We enabled them to be merciful toward one another and to innovate monasticism and originate it." It is excessive devotion to worship through asceticism and withdrawal from people. Its meaning is the act attributed to the monks (rahban), who are the fearful ones; it is the pattern fa'lan, from rahiba, like khashyan from khashiya. It is also read with a damma on the ra' (رُهْبانِيَّةً), as if it were a relative form (nisbah) to ruhban, which is the plural of rahib, like rakib and rukban. The cause of their innovating it was that the tyrants prevailed over the believers after the raising of Jesus, peace be upon him, and they fought them three times, until only a few of them remained. They feared that they would be seduced in their religion, so they chose monasticism on the peaks of mountains, fleeing with their religion, sincerely devoting themselves to worship.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We did not prescribe it for them﴾ is a resumed clause (jumlah mustanifah). It was also said that it is another adjective for "rahbaniyyah." The negation on the first reading is directed at the very origin of the act. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except seeking the good pleasure of Allah﴾ is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'): that is, "We did not impose it upon them ourselves at all, but they invented it seeking the good pleasure of Allah." Then He censures them with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But they did not observe it with its proper observance﴾, since a vow (nadhr) is a covenant with Allah that may not be broken, especially when it is intended for His good pleasure, exalted is He. On the second reading, the negation is directed at its qualifier and not at the act itself, and the exception is connected (istithna' muttasil) from the most general of causes, meaning: "We did not prescribe it for them by enabling them to invent it for any reason except that they might seek by it the good pleasure of Allah and merit reward by it. It is necessarily part of this that they should maintain it and observe it with its proper observance. But they did not all observe it, only some of them did."

﴿So We gave those among them who believed﴾ true faith, which is belief in the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, after observing their monasticism, not merely observing it, for after the mission (ba'thah) it is pure futility (laghw mahd) and absolute disbelief, and how could it bring reward?

﴿their reward.﴾ That is: the reward that is specific to them.

﴿But many of them are defiant (fasiqun).﴾ That is: they went beyond the limits of following. Interpreting the two groups as referring to those of the past who observed the rights of monasticism before abrogation (naskh), and those who, at that time, neglected it by adopting trinitarianism, the belief in incarnation (ittihad), and seeking reputation, without addressing their belief in the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, or their disbelief in him, is something the context does not support.

O you who believe, (i.e., in the earlier messengers):

Fear Allah (regarding what He has forbidden you).

And believe in His Messenger (i.e., in Muhammad (ﷺ)). The fact that he is mentioned without qualification indicates that he is the unique (ʿalam fard) in the messengership, such that the mind does not turn to anyone else.

He will give you a double portion (kiflayn, meaning two shares) of His mercy, for your belief in the Messenger and in those messengers before him, upon them be prayers and peace, but not in the sense that their law remains in force after the mission of Muhammad; rather, [it is in the sense] that it was true before abrogation (naskh).

And He will make for you a light by which you will walk (on the Day of Resurrection), as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Their light will run before them and on their right hands﴾.

And He will forgive you (the disbelief and sins you committed in the past).

And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful (i.e., exceedingly so in forgiveness and mercy).

And the phrase of Him, exalted is He: ﴿so that the People of the Book may know﴾ is connected to the implied content of the imperative clause, which carries the meaning of a condition (*shart*). The intended sense is: "If you fear Allah and believe in His Messenger, He will give you such-and-such, so that those among the People of the Book who did not submit may not know," that is, so that they may know. The "lā" is extra (*mazīdah*), as indicated by the reading *liya'lama*, and by the readings *likay yaʿlama* and *li-an yaʿlama*, with the nūn assimilated into the yā'. The "anna" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that they have no power over anything of Allah's bounty﴾, is the light form (*mukhaffafah*) of the heavy "inna," whose noun, which is the dummy pronoun (*ḍamīr al-sha'n*), is omitted. The clause in its position is in the accusative, as the object of *yaʿlama*, meaning: so that they may know that they will obtain none of what has been mentioned of His bounty, of the double portion, the light, and the forgiveness, and that they cannot attain it, since they have not fulfilled its condition, which is belief in His Messenger. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that the bounty is in the hand of Allah﴾, is conjoined to "that they have no power," and His saying: ﴿He gives it to whom He wills﴾ is a second predicate of "anna." It was also said that it is the predicate, and the prepositional phrase is a necessary circumstantial clause (*ḥāl lāzimah*). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and Allah is the Lord of mighty bounty﴾ is a concluding parenthetical statement (*i'tirāḍ tadhyīlī*) confirming the content of what precedes it.

It is also permissible that the command to piety and faith is addressed to other than the People of the Book. The meaning then is: fear Allah and remain steadfast in your faith in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and He will give you what He promised to those among the People of the Book who believed, of the double portion, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice﴾, and He will not diminish for you from the like of their reward, because you are like them in the two beliefs, not distinguishing between any of His messengers. It is related that the believers among the People of the Book boasted over the rest of the believers that they would be given their reward twice, and claimed superiority over them, so this was revealed.

"Liyalā" was also read, with the hamza changed to yā' because it is vowelled with fatḥah after a kasrah. It was read with the yā' sukūn and fatḥah on the lām, like a woman's name, and with kasrah on the lām with sukūn on the yā'. "An lā yaqdirū" was also read.

This is what has been said. It has also been said that "lā" is not extra, and the pronoun of "lā yaqdirūn" refers to the Prophet (p-215) (peace and blessings be upon him) and his companions. The meaning is: so that the People of the Book do not believe that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and those who believe in him have no power over anything of Allah's bounty, which is an expression for what they have been given of the happiness of both abodes, on the basis that their not knowing of their lack of power over that is a metaphor (*kināyah*) for their knowing of their power over it. Thus His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that the bounty is in the hand of Allah﴾ … etc. is conjoined to "that they may not know."

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Sūrat al-Ḥadīd, he will be recorded among those who believed in Allah and His messengers."
